transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jared Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Leah Morales (CTO - Aurora), Ravi Patel (Head Infra), Anika Bose (Security Lead), Tom Hsu (ML Platform)

Auto-summary (auto gen, rough):
Aurora is scoping a POC to validate Redwood Private with PrivateLink (AWS) and strict egress rules (no public internet egress from model traffic). They want to run a 2-week pilot validating latency and cost against a representative workload, with success criteria around p99 latency and throughput, and legal review of data residency. Action items assigned for network diagrams, IP allowlists, and a bench window.

Topics:
- PrivateLink vs VPC peering tradeoffs
- Regional residency (us-east-1 vs eu-west-1) and multi-region routing
- Egress constraints: forced proxy, NAT egress, no internet egress allowed for model payloads
- Bench plan: dataset, qps pattern, model family (Llama-like vs open LLM), quantization and dedicated capacity
- Success criteria: p99 latency target, throughput, error rate, cost per 1M tokens

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, Jared from Redwood. Thanks for making time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Leah: Yeah hi, Leah here, CTO at Aurora Biotech. We've got Ravi, Anika, and Tom with me.
[00:12] Ravi: Hi, morning.
[00:14] Tom: Hey all.
[00:15] Maya: Maya from Redwood infra team, focusing on Private deployments and networking.

[00:30] Jared: Thanks. The goal today is scoping the POC for PrivateLink and the egress constraints you mentioned in the RFI. We want to be clear on success criteria, workload size, bench windows, plus any legal/regulatory redlines. Leah, are the residency constraints per data type or whole account?
[00:45] Leah: Good question. It's mostly PHI-adjacent analytics, so we need model inputs to remain in-region for storage and processing. For the POC, target region is us-east-1 but if things look good we'll add eu-west-1 later. Also, absolutely no unrestricted egress for inference payloads out to the public internet.
[01:05] Maya: Understood. We support PrivateLink endpoints in AWS; that means we can expose a VPC endpoint service in your VPC and you can keep traffic on the AWS backbone. That avoids internet egress.
[01:18] Anika: Quick clarifying Q — do you need VPC peering for metrics or logs, or can logs go to a central S3 in our logging account via PrivateLink too?
[01:28] Maya: Good point — we usually recommend using PrivateLink for the inference API traffic and S3/vended logs can go through a cross-account role. We can also push audit logs to your KMS-encrypted bucket via PrivateLink — minimal peering required. But if you have existing peering topology that simplifies routing, peering is supported.
[01:48] Ravi: Our infra team prefers no new long-lived peering links; PrivateLink is preferred for security reasons. We also run a forced egress proxy for all outbound traffic, so we need Redwood to talk to the proxy or be allowed through NAT.
[02:03] Maya: We can support proxy traversal. For the POC we can either establish an outbound-to-proxy configuration, or we can set up PrivateLink so there's no internet path. If your proxy inspects TLS, we need to coordinate certs.
[02:20] Tom: On the benchmarks — we want to replicate our production QPS. It's a bursty profile: baseline 10 rps with spikes to 120 rps during batch processing windows. Typical request sizes average 600 tokens in, 350 tokens out. We plan a synthetic corpus of 50k tokens for the bench.
[02:42] Jared: Great, that gives us numbers. Our suggestion for the POC: a two-stage run — a functional week to validate connectivity, auth, and logging; then a 1-day stress benchmark with your spike profile. For models, do you have a preferred family?
[02:58] Leah: We are evaluating a mix. Ideally something cost-effective but high-quality. We want to test an opt-quantized Llama-2 style small-medium model and a higher-quality 7B variant. The idea is to measure cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:13] Maya: We'll suggest a pair of instance+quantized model profiles. For a p99 latency target, what would you consider acceptable?
[03:20] Leah: For interactive endpoints we want p99 under 400 ms if possible — but we know that's aggressive with large context. For the POC, a p99 under 600 ms for the 600-token requests is acceptable; production target could be tightened.
[03:36] Jared: Noted. We'll include p50/p95/p99 in the bench report. Also error budget — what's acceptable error rate?
[03:42] Ravi: Under 1% errors during bench. Anything more and we'll flag stability issues.
[03:47] Anika: Security checklist — SOC 2 report, key management options (we require AWS KMS integration), and support for customer-managed keys for logs.
[03:58] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and support external KMS/HSM for Private deployments. For PrivateLink, logs can be KMS-encrypted in your account using cross-account encryption. We'll share the specific security pack.
[04:12] Tom: About data residency: during inference, are model weights ever staged in another region or pulled from a central model registry? We need assurance weights stay in-region for Private deployments.
[04:25] Maya: For Redwood Private on dedicated capacity in your VPC, model artifacts can be pinned to the region. Our control plane will orchestrate images but for Private deployments we can keep weights in your account or on regional storage. For hosted variants we sometimes pull from central registry, but that won't be part of this POC.
[04:43] Leah: Good. For the POC we want everything in us-east-1 and confirm no cross-region replication.
[04:51] Jared: We'll document that in the POC scope. Now networking specifics — Ravi, can you share the egress architecture?
[05:00] Ravi: Sure. We have a forced egress proxy cluster (envoy) in the shared-services VPC; all outbound goes via the proxy which performs TLS inspection. No direct internet allowed from compute subnets. We can either allow traffic to a PrivateLink endpoint or we can create an exception for the proxy to allow outbound to Redwood egress IPs via NAT.
[05:21] Maya: For PrivateLink we put an NLB in our service VPC and you create an interface endpoint in your VPC — your traffic never leaves AWS backbone. That avoids your proxy needing to see outbound calls, provided your security policy allows endpoint services. Otherwise we can provide an egress IP list that your proxy will allow.
[05:40] Anika: Does PrivateLink support mutual TLS? We need mTLS for service-to-service in some cases.
[05:46] Maya: We support TLS and can front with mutual TLS—work requires cert exchange. We'll note the cert process in the network doc.
[05:55] Tom: For benchmarking we'll need some metrics collection — can Redwood push Prometheus metrics to our scraping stack, or do we need to ingest?
[06:04] Maya: We can expose Prom metrics on an internal endpoint that you can scrape over the endpoint, or push metrics to your CloudWatch account via cross-account role. For the POC scrapes are easiest.
[06:15] Jared: Okay, action items are forming. I also want to raise cost expectations: POC pricing for dedicated capacity is usually a short-term reserved pool — we'll propose a 2-week commit. Is that acceptable?
[06:27] Leah: Yes, budget approved for a 2-week pilot. We'll need an estimate up front to sign off.
[06:33] Jared: We'll send a pricing sheet with the bench-config and estimated cost per 1M tokens.
[06:38] Ravi: One more practical — our security team insists on an egress IP allowlist rather than opening up broad endpoint policies; will you provide a stable set of egress IPs for the POC?
[06:49] Maya: We can provide a small set of egress IPs for the NLB in the endpoint service, but PrivateLink avoids the internet egress path; still, we'll give you IPs to allow if you want the proxy exception path. Note that IP ranges can change with scaling; we'll provide an SLA'd range for the POC window.
[07:07] Anika: Also need logging retention controls — logs must be retained for 7 years for compliance, can Redwood ship logs to our encrypted S3 with lifecycle rules?
[07:18] Maya: Yes, S3 delivery with KMS encryption and lifecycle rules is supported. We'll include the CloudTrail/audit and per-request trace output in the security pack.
[07:28] Tom: Bench harness — we'll provide a CSV of requests and a qps script; would Redwood run the bench from your side or do we run it from our infra to simulate client traffic?
[07:38] Jared: We recommend Aurora drives the client-side traffic to mimic real network path; Redwood will provide an optional runner in our bench harness repo. For PrivateLink the traffic should originate from your VPC to accurately exercise the endpoint.
[07:53] Ravi: Fine. We'll run the traffic. We'll need a test account/credentials and instructions.
[07:58] Maya: We'll provide ephemeral creds scoped to the bench, and RBAC roles for access.
[08:05] Leah: Timeline — if we do functional week next week, and bench the following week, we can have results and go/no-go in three weeks. Is that realistic?
[08:15] Maya: Yes — a staging week plus a stress day. We'll need network changes (endpoint creation, proxy allowlist) early in the functional week.
[08:25] Jared: I'll draft the POC schedule and SOPs and circulate.
[08:30] Anika: For SOC2 and KMS paperwork, can you send the security pack to our legal slack channel?
[08:36] Maya: Yes, will send to legal and security.
[08:39] Ravi: Security also asked about model artifact access logs — who can see model inputs/outputs?
[08:46] Maya: Access is RBAC controlled; by default only service accounts used by Redwood infra see raw payloads for debugging; for Private deployments we can restrict that to a customer-controlled audit role and provide audit logs to your account. We'll include the exact audit fields in the security pack.
[09:05] Tom: Small thing — how do rollbacks during POC work if we see a regression in output quality between quantized and full model?
[09:12] Jared: We'll run A/B with canary routing; if quality drops we'll revert traffic to the fallback model. That can be automated in the POC config.
[09:20] Leah: Sounds good.
[09:22] Maya: I'll also attach a small network diagram showing PrivateLink flow, our NLB, and the endpoint ENIs, plus sample CFN.
[09:31] Jared: Okay let's recap real quick and confirm next steps.
[09:35] Jared: Redwood will: 1) send PrivateLink setup doc + CFN (Maya), 2) provide bench harness + pricing estimates (Jared), 3) provide egress IP list if you choose NAT proxy exception (Maya).
[09:49] Leah: Aurora will: 1) provide IP allowlist/proxy details (Ravi), 2) prepare the test corpus and traffic scripts (Tom), 3) identify legal/security reviewer (Anika/Leah).
[10:05] Jared: Great. Proposed bench window: 2025-06-02, 10:00-12:00 UTC. Does that work?
[10:12] Leah: Tentatively yes, subject to calendar.
[10:15] Ravi: We'll confirm by 2025-05-27.
[10:18] Maya: I'll email the docs by 2025-05-23.
[10:21] Jared: And I'll send pricing and the success criteria doc by tomorrow 2025-05-22.
[10:27] Anika: Thanks. One note — please call out any possible egress vectors in the docs. We need explicit confirmation of "no internet egress" for inference payloads during the POC.
[10:38] Maya: We'll include a checklist and a signed statement for the POC scope about egress paths.
[10:45] Leah: Alright thanks everyone.
[10:47] Jared: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the items.
[10:50] [meeting ends]
